source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

candidates.name: LLM-as-a-judge
candidates.summary: Using a language model to grade another model's outputs against criteria or a rubric. An agentic variant lets the judge call tools to inspect the artifact before deciding.
candidates.evidence: graded by an agentic LLM judge that interacts with the output workbook

candidates.name: Rubric-based evaluation
candidates.summary: Scoring complex outputs against a set of fine-grained, usually binary yes/no criteria with point weights. This suits tasks whose quality cannot be checked by a single programmatic test.

candidates.name: Krippendorff's alpha
candidates.summary: A statistic for inter-annotator agreement that corrects for chance and works with any number of raters and data types. Values near 1 mean strong agreement.

candidates.name: Macro-averaged F1 score
candidates.summary: The F1 score (harmonic mean of precision and recall) computed separately for each class and then averaged with equal weight. It treats all classes equally regardless of frequency.

candidates.name: Perturbation testing
candidates.summary: Changing an input of a model or workbook and checking that dependent outputs recompute to the correct new values. It reveals hardcoded values and broken dependency links.
candidates.evidence: A perturbation criterion specifies an input mutation

candidates.name: Agentic evaluation harness
candidates.summary: The scaffold that gives a language model agent a set of tools and a loop for taking actions in an environment, logging each step. A uniform harness makes results comparable across models.
candidates.evidence: an agentic harness of 20 tools organized into six categories

candidates.name: Tool-using language model agent
candidates.summary: A language model that works toward a goal by repeatedly choosing and calling external tools, such as reading and writing files or running code, and observing the results.
candidates.evidence: tasks LLM agents with synthesis, manipulation, and comprehension tasks

candidates.name: Spreadsheet formula dependencies
candidates.summary: Spreadsheet cells reference one another via formulas, forming a dependency graph through which changes propagate. Hardcoding a computed value instead of linking breaks this propagation.
candidates.evidence: Models that hardcode intermediate values, erroneously overwrite a formula cell with a constant

candidates.name: Discounted cash flow valuation
candidates.summary: A valuation method that estimates a company's value as the present value of its projected future free cash flows plus a terminal value, discounted at a rate such as WACC.

candidates.name: Weighted average cost of capital
candidates.summary: The blended required return on a firm's debt and equity, weighted by their proportions in its capital structure. It is commonly used as the discount rate in valuation.

candidates.name: Debt schedule and cash sweep
candidates.summary: A financial model section tracking debt tranche balances, interest and repayments over time. A cash sweep applies excess cash to repay debt, often creating circular references with interest.
candidates.evidence: Build a debt schedule section at the bottom of the uploaded worksheet

candidates.name: Circular reference with iterative calculation
candidates.summary: A circular reference occurs when a formula depends on its own result, directly or indirectly, as with interest on average debt balances. Iterative calculation repeatedly recomputes until values converge.
candidates.evidence: iterative-calc enabled so debt schedules and LBO-style circular references converge correctly

candidates.name: Pareto frontier
candidates.summary: The set of options for which no other option is both cheaper and better. Options off the frontier are dominated.

candidates.name: Programmatic verifiability of evaluation
candidates.summary: The property that a task's output can be checked by executable tests or exact-match comparison. Tasks with subjective or multi-dimensional quality are hard to verify this way.
candidates.evidence: difficult to verify programmatically but can be reliably evaluated by an LM judge

candidates.name: Minimal-elicitation prompting
candidates.summary: Evaluating models with a brief prompt lacking workflow prescriptions or tool preferences, to isolate underlying capability from instruction-following effects.
candidates.evidence: we adopt a minimal-elicitation prompt (61 words

candidates.name: Code execution sandbox
candidates.summary: An isolated environment that runs untrusted code with restricted built-ins, allow-listed imports and timeouts, preventing file, network and system access.
candidates.evidence: restricted built-ins and a tight import whitelist

candidates.name: Benchmark data leakage and held-out sets
candidates.summary: Keeping part of a benchmark private so models cannot be trained on its test items, which would inflate scores.
candidates.evidence: We retain a private set primarily out of potential leakage concerns

candidates.name: Inter-annotator agreement
candidates.summary: The degree to which independent human raters assign the same labels to the same items. It sets a ceiling on how well an automatic judge can be expected to agree with humans.
candidates.evidence: near the human IRR reliability ceiling

candidates.name: Financial modeling conventions
candidates.summary: Standard practices for structuring spreadsheet financial models, such as separating inputs, linking rather than hardcoding, consistent formatting and error checks.
